prohibited_recommendations: Do not withhold IV thrombolysis because of the isolated aPTT of 46 s, or wait for antiphospholipid results: she takes no anticoagulant, INR is 0.94 and platelets are 138 x10^9/L.
Do not give sumatriptan, now or later: triptans are contraindicated after ischemic stroke and in antiphospholipid syndrome.

Do not diagnose complicated or hemiplegic migraine and send her home: persistent aphasia and arm weakness that began as the aura faded, with a headache unlike her usual one, are a stroke until imaging shows otherwise.
Do not use a DOAC for secondary prevention if antiphospholipid syndrome is confirmed: warfarin (INR 2 to 3) is the anticoagulant.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (onset of the visual aura, about 70 minutes before arrival; the aphasia and right arm weakness followed about 20 minutes later as the aura faded) and the NIHSS (6: facial palsy 1, visual 1 for extinction, right arm 1, sensory 1, language 1, extinction 1).

IV thrombolysis: give (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, maximum 90 mg, or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg, maximum 25 mg), because she is within 4.5 hours with a disabling deficit (aphasia and right arm weakness) and no contraindication: glucose 88 mg/dL, INR 0.94, platelets 138 x10^9/L, no anticoagulant exposure. The isolated aPTT of 46 s, with no anticoagulant and no bleeding history, does not justify withholding it or waiting for antiphospholipid results. Thrombectomy: not indicated (no occlusion on CTA).
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes; keep blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis (152/74 on arrival) and below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after.

Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours; give no antiplatelet, anticoagulant or NSAID for 24 hours after thrombolysis, until follow-up imaging excludes hemorrhage.

Stop sumatriptan permanently (contraindicated after ischemic stroke and in antiphospholipid syndrome) and stop ibuprofen; use paracetamol for headache and review migraine prophylaxis with a non-vasoconstrictive agent.

Send antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I) before any anticoagulant is started, and repeat them at 12 weeks to confirm persistence (Sydney criteria).

Once 24-hour imaging excludes hemorrhage, start aspirin; if antiphospholipid syndrome is confirmed at 12 weeks, switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3 (AHA/ASA 2021; EULAR 2019); do not use a DOAC (rivaroxaban was inferior to warfarin in triple-positive APS).

Refer to rheumatology and hematology for APS management and SLE screening (mother with SLE; ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement normal now), and counsel that estrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated and that warfarin is teratogenic, so any pregnancy needs specialist planning.
Increase levothyroxine for the TSH of 8.3 mIU/L and recheck thyroid function in 6 to 8 weeks.

key_clinical_evidence: The migraine history is the trap: her usual aura is followed by a severe headache after it resolves, whereas this time aphasia and right arm weakness began as the scotoma faded and persisted with only a mild headache. Persistent focal deficits in a migraineur are a stroke until imaging shows otherwise.

Last known well is the onset of the aura, about 70 minutes before arrival. NIHSS 6 (facial palsy 1, visual 1, right arm 1, sensory 1, language 1, extinction 1) with aphasia and arm weakness is a disabling deficit within 4.5 hours, and CT shows no haemorrhage: she is a thrombolysis candidate. CTA shows no occlusion, so thrombectomy does not apply.

The aPTT of 46 s is isolated (INR 0.94, platelets 138 x10^9/L) in a woman who takes no anticoagulant and has no bleeding history. The thrombolysis decision is made on those values, without waiting for antiphospholipid tests that take hours to days; a lupus anticoagulant, suspected from the prior miscarriage and the mother's SLE, prolongs the aPTT in vitro without causing bleeding.

The antiphospholipid panel then shows triple positivity (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG 90.9 GPL and IgM 23.7 MPL, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG and IgM), which explains the aPTT and is the highest-risk antibody profile; with ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement normal, primary APS is the provisional mechanism.

Classification requires the antibodies to persist at 12 weeks. A single first-trimester miscarriage does not meet the obstetric criterion, but with the family history it should have prompted testing earlier.
Normal CTA, a normal echocardiogram without Libman-Sacks lesions or shunt, and sinus rhythm on 48-hour monitoring exclude the competing mechanisms.

Secondary prevention: aspirin after 24-hour imaging, then warfarin (INR 2 to 3) once APS is confirmed; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS (TRAPS). Starting warfarin first would also interfere with lupus anticoagulant testing at 12 weeks.
Sumatriptan is a vasoconstrictor and is contraindicated after ischemic stroke and in antiphospholipid syndrome; she wanted to take it for this event.

clinical_pearls: Migraine with aura and acute ischemic stroke can be indistinguishable in the first 30 minutes — DWI MRI is the only reliable discriminator; always pursue stroke workup when deficits are motor or aphasic

Lupus anticoagulant prolongs the PTT in vitro by interfering with phospholipid-dependent assay steps but is a pro-thrombotic antibody in vivo — it is the strongest individual predictor of APS-related thrombosis

Triple-positive APS (all three antibody classes positive simultaneously) is the highest-risk APS profile and mandates indefinite anticoagulation; DOACs have demonstrated higher failure rates than warfarin in APS-related thrombosis

Obstetric APS criteria (recurrent miscarriage, fetal loss, placental insufficiency) are frequently missed prior to a thrombotic event — a history of unexplained miscarriage in a young woman with stroke should trigger APS workup

APS affects approximately 10-20% of young adults with cryptogenic ischemic stroke — it is one of the most important treatable stroke mechanisms in patients under 50 with no traditional vascular risk factors
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — 43-year-old left-handed Hispanic woman with migraine-with-aura history presenting with right arm weakness and anomic aphasia. Patient and bystanders initially attribute symptoms to complicated migraine. MRI DWI confirms acute left MCA cortical infarct. Paradoxically prolonged PTT and mild thrombocytopenia create compounding decision-points. Systematic workup including antiphospholipid panel reveals triple-positive APS as the underlying mechanism. Real case seeded from Cureus 2024 (PMID 38659540), a 43-year-old woman with triple-positive APS and left MCA territory ischemic stroke.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Triple-positive APS as hidden stroke mechanism in a migraineur; paradoxical PTT prolongation that mimics anticoagulation; mild thrombocytopenia distracting from APS; normal vascular imaging and cardiac workup; requires antiphospholipid panel to unlock diagnosis.
metadata.real_seed_note: Case seeded from: Cureus 2024 (PMC11042755, PMID 38659540, CC-BY 4.0). Original case: 43-year-old woman, triple-positive APS (lupus anticoagulant dRVVT 1.92/1.97, anticardiolipin IgG 90.9 GPL, IgM 23.7 MPL, anti-B2GP1 IgG 21.0, IgM 10.0 U/mL), acute left MCA cortical infarct (left superior parietal and posterior insula), treated with IV alteplase with improvement to NIHSS 0. Antiphospholipid antibody values, ECG (normal sinus rhythm), echo (normal), and lipid panel adapted directly from the published case. Demographics, HPI, migraine history, miscarriage history, family history of SLE, and red herring elements authored for NeuroBench narrative fidelity and puzzle construction.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Elena Vargas is a 43-year-old left-handed Hispanic woman with a history of migraine with visual aura and hypothyroidism who presents to the emergency department with acute-onset word-finding difficulty and right arm weakness of approximately 50 minutes duration. She was at home grading papers when she noticed a zig-zag visual scotoma in her right visual field, which she recognized as her typical migraine aura. Approximately 20 minutes later, as the visual symptoms were fading, she noticed she was unable to retrieve common words — she reached for a pen but could not name it and instead said 'the thing you write with.' Simultaneously, she noticed her right arm felt heavy and clumsy, with difficulty gripping her pen. Unlike her usual migraine headache (which begins after the aura resolves and is severe and throbbing), the current headache is mild — rated 3/10. Her husband, who has witnessed her prior migraines, became alarmed because her previous auras have never caused arm weakness or speech changes and called 911. En route to hospital, EMS documented mild word-finding difficulty and right arm drift. The patient insisted she 'just needs to take her sumatriptan.' She explicitly denies chest pain, palpitations, diplopia, vertigo, dysphagia, facial numbness, loss of consciousness, or prior episodes of arm weakness. She has had no recent illness, fever, or trauma. She reports one prior first-trimester miscarriage at age 38 that was never investigated. Her mother was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus at age 45. A maternal aunt had a deep vein thrombosis at age 40. The patient takes sumatriptan for migraines and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She is a non-smoker, consumes minimal alcohol, is physically active, and has no known cardiovascular risk factors. She is not on oral contraceptives.
